lead: A Maxwell relation turns an entropy slope, which cannot be measured, into a pressure-volume-temperature slope, which can. It exists because each of the four potentials U, H, A and G has an exact differential, and exactness forces its two cross-derivatives to be equal. Four potentials give four relations. With the TdS equations they give entropy, internal energy and enthalpy changes of real gases and liquids from p–v–T data alone, which is how steam and refrigerant tables are built.
prereq: You need: the exactness test of Exact differentials, reciprocity and cyclic relations, and the four differentials of Gibbs and Helmholtz functions.

sections.h3: From an exact differential to a Maxwell relation

blocks.text: Start with dU = T dS − p dV. It has the form M dx + N dy with x = S, M = T, y = V and N = −p. The exactness test (∂M/∂y)<sub>x</sub> = (∂N/∂x)<sub>y</sub> gives at once

blocks.where: The left side is the rate of change of temperature with volume at constant entropy; the right side is minus the rate of change of pressure with entropy at constant volume.

blocks.text: That is the first Maxwell relation. It is not a new law, only the exactness of dU written out. The same steps work for every potential:

items: Pick the potential whose natural variables match the slope you want: U(S, V), H(S, p), A(T, V) or G(T, p).
Write its differential and read the coefficients M and N, with their signs.
Apply the exactness test, keeping every minus sign in front of a coefficient.
Check the subscripts: they must be the natural variables of that potential.

sections.h3: The four relations and entropy from p–v–T data

blocks.text: The last two hold T fixed and put entropy on the left, so they are the working relations: (∂s/∂v)<sub>T</sub> = (∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> and (∂s/∂p)<sub>T</sub> = −(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>, per unit mass. Their right-hand sides are slopes of an equation of state or of a table. For an ideal gas, v = RT/p gives (∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = R/p, so (∂s/∂p)<sub>T</sub> = −R/p and an isothermal change gives Δs = −R·ln(p₂/p₁).
Figure 4.5.1 shows the A relation at work for carbon dioxide: the slope of each constant-volume line on a p–T diagram is the rate at which entropy grows with volume at that temperature.
Write s = s(T, v) and s = s(T, p), use cv = T(∂s/∂T)v and cp = T(∂s/∂T)p, and replace the entropy slopes by Maxwell relations. This gives the two TdS equations:
First TdS equation: c<sub>v</sub> in kJ/(kg·K); the slope (∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> comes from the equation of state.
Second TdS equation: c<sub>p</sub> in kJ/(kg·K); the slope (∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> is measured at constant pressure.
Put the first into du = T ds − p dv and the second into dh = T ds + v dp:
The bracket is how internal energy changes with volume at constant temperature.
The bracket is how enthalpy changes with pressure at constant temperature.

For an ideal gas both brackets are zero (T·R/v − p = 0 and v − T·R/p = 0), so u and h depend on temperature alone. For a real gas they are not zero, which is why steam tables need pressure as well as temperature. The enthalpy bracket also gives the Joule-Thomson coefficient, and the two TdS equations together give cp − cv (see Expansivity, compressibility, Mayer relation and Joule-Thomson coefficient).

examples.question: Air (ideal gas, R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K)) is compressed isothermally at 300 K from 1 bar to 5 bar. Use a Maxwell relation to find the entropy change per kg.
steps: The slope needed links s, p and T, so use the G relation: (∂s/∂p)<sub>T</sub> = −(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>.
For an ideal gas v = RT/p, so (∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = R/p.
Hence (∂s/∂p)<sub>T</sub> = −R/p, and at constant T, ds = −R dp/p.
Integrate from 1 bar to 5 bar: Δs = −R·ln(p₂/p₁) = −0.287 × ln 5 = −0.287 × 1.6094 = −0.4619 kJ/(kg·K).
The sign is negative: squeezing the gas into a smaller volume at constant temperature lowers its entropy.

examples.question: 1 mol of carbon dioxide, treated as a van der Waals gas with a = 0.364 Pa·m⁶/mol² and b = 4.27 × 10⁻⁵ m³/mol, expands isothermally at 300 K from 0.001 to 0.002 m³/mol. Use Maxwell relations to find Δs and Δu, and compare Δs with the ideal-gas value. R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
steps: Equation of state: p = RT/(v − b) − a/v². At constant v: (∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> = R/(v − b).
Ideal gas: Δs = R·ln(v₂/v₁) = 8.314 × 0.6931 = 5.763 J/(mol·K). The real gas gains about 3.2 % more, because the molecules' own volume b takes up part of the space.
Energy relation: (∂u/∂v)<sub>T</sub> = T(∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> − p = RT/(v − b) − [RT/(v − b) − a/v²] = a/v².
examples.answer: Δs = 5.946 J/(mol·K), against 5.763 J/(mol·K) for an ideal gas, and Δu = +182 J/mol: the gas stores energy as its molecules move apart against their attraction, where an ideal gas would have Δu = 0.

traps: Sign slip: (∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = (∂p/∂T)<sub>V</sub> and (∂T/∂p)<sub>S</sub> = (∂V/∂S)<sub>p</sub> have no minus; the U and G relations do. Writing (∂s/∂p)<sub>T</sub> = +(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> is the commonest error, so derive from the potential instead of memorising.
Wrong subscript: the held variable must be a natural variable of the potential you started from. (∂s/∂p)<sub>T</sub> comes from G.
Mixing V and v in one problem. The relations hold for total volume (m³) or specific volume (m³/kg), and a mix costs a factor of the mass.
Using the relations for a system that does magnetic, electrical or surface work. They belong to a simple compressible system with two independent properties.
Saying du = c<sub>v</sub>dT for every substance. That holds for an ideal gas or at constant volume; a real gas adds [T(∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> − p]dv.

quiz.q: Write the Maxwell relation that comes from dA = −S dT − p dV.

quiz.a: T ds = c<sub>v</sub>dT + T(∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub>dv and T ds = c<sub>p</sub>dT − T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>dp.

quiz.q: Why is a Maxwell relation useful in practice?
quiz.a: It replaces an entropy slope, which cannot be measured directly, by a p–v–T slope that can be measured or read from an equation of state or a table.

quiz.q: Air (R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K)) is compressed isothermally at 350 K from 1 bar to 10 bar. Find Δs per kg.
Show that (∂h/∂p)<sub>T</sub> = 0 for an ideal gas.
quiz.a: (∂h/∂p)<sub>T</sub> = v − T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub>. With v = RT/p, T(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = RT/p = v, so the bracket is zero: h depends on T only.

quiz.q: For a van der Waals gas show that (∂u/∂v)<sub>T</sub> = a/v².
quiz.a: (∂u/∂v)<sub>T</sub> = T(∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> − p = RT/(v − b) − RT/(v − b) + a/v² = a/v².

quiz.q: Why does the entropy of a van der Waals gas rise more than that of an ideal gas in the same isothermal expansion?
quiz.a: (∂s/∂v)<sub>T</sub> = R/(v − b) is larger than R/v, because only v − b is free space. In the carbon dioxide example Δs is 5.946 against 5.763 J/(mol·K).

beyond: Modern steam and refrigerant tables are computed from one fundamental equation, the Helmholtz function as a function of density and temperature, and every entry, entropy included, comes out by differentiating it with the same mixed-derivative logic. The IAPWS formulation for water works this way. Search next: fundamental equation of state, IAPWS-95, departure functions.

figure.caption: Constant-volume lines of carbon dioxide as a van der Waals gas: each is straight, and by the Maxwell relation its slope R/(v − b), 8.68 kPa/K at 0.001 m³/mol and 4.25 kPa/K at 0.002 m³/mol, is the rate at which entropy grows with volume at fixed temperature.

spec.aria: Pressure against temperature from 300 to 350 K for two volumes of carbon dioxide, 0.001 and 0.002 cubic metres per mole. Both lines are straight, with slopes 8.68 and 4.25 kPa per kelvin. At 300 K the pressures are 2.24 and 1.18 MPa; expanding from the first state to the second raises entropy by 5.946 J per mol K.
